# Energy and climate model: results

*Generated by `models/tools/energy/run.py` (run by `run-all.sh`); do not edit by hand. What the model is, its evidence and its limits are in `MODEL-CARD.md`. Status: **working**.*

Every case below is the decided clean power set built up one layer at a time against the January 2029 current law, then the options memo 1 weighed and the sensitivities. The permitting package is not assumed except in the rows that say so. Energy CO2 is against EIA's 2005 level (5,999 Mt); net greenhouse gases against EPA's (6,536 Mt).

**Uncertainty** (the carbon model's uncertain inputs, 60 draws, 10th-90th percentile): the decided set is 40%-42% below 2005 in 2035 and 65%-67% in 2050. Published models disagree by more than this for the same policy (EMF 32: 26-47% for one tax in 2030; survey.md, 2.9), so treat the band as a floor on the uncertainty.

**The clean electricity standard.** On the decided set clean power reaches 73% of generation in 2035 against the 80% target, and 87% in 2040 against 100%: suppliers short of credits pay the capped payment, about $163 billion over FY2030-39 ($74 billion with the permitting package). Grid access, not price, limits wind and solar building in the engine (SRC-0077, v2.4), so the standard works mainly as a floor and a source of bill-protection money; memo 3's figure of about $0.05 trillion was on the legacy model with the permitting package assumed and the 80% target only.

Point 1's goal is 61-66% below 2005 in 2035 (net); the decided set reaches about 43%, as section 3 of the dossier says plainly that no modeled package reaches the range.

## For clean power's re-review (`DEC-2026-11-13-12`; the list in #346)

1. **The 100%-by-2040 standard.** Clean power reaches 73% in 2035, 87% in 2040 and 92% in 2045, held back by grid access, not price. Suppliers short of credits pay about $163 billion over FY2030-39 and $41 billion in FY2040 ($74 billion over FY2030-39 with the permitting package). #346 carries about $110 billion and $29 billion in 2040 from the legacy model, which assumes the permitting package in every run and reaches 91% in 2040; this model does not assume the package, and with it the payments fall to the figure in brackets, below #346's; the two models also differ in grid build (here the standby builder adds lines) and in the target path (100% by 2040 here). Retail electricity in 2040 is 16.1 cents a kWh against 14.7 under current law (2025 dollars, national average).
2. **Memo 1 B's narrower price.** Receipts and the dividend are in the next table: about $405 an adult in 2035 (#346: about $439). Energy CO2 is 41% below 2005 in 2035 and net greenhouse gases 43%, inside the dossier's judged 40-48%. Buildings emit 469 Mt in 2035 with the clean-heat standard and no price, against 450 Mt under memo 1 A's economy-wide price.
3. **Bills by region.** Not answered: the engine is one national market. The households table below is by income; a regional split needs the household model's state codes and regional generation mixes, a later step.
4. **The coal and gas fleets' wind-down** (GW of capacity, and TWh generated in brackets), for the guarantee's count of covered closures:

5. **The credits against the booking.** The engine counts about $1,037 billion over FY2030-39 (the standby builder adds about $141 billion of it: its own program cost at half strength, which the engine counts with the credits, and the extra credited wind, solar and storage its lines connect) against the booked CLI-1 of $757 billion; a cross-check, not a score.
6. **Outside runs.** BL-3 and PK-1 in the benchmarks compare with Espen's Energy Policy Simulator runs.

The transition guarantee (memo 7 B, CLI-11, with tribal governments' lost revenue, DEC-2026-11-13-11) is a fiscal program the dossier prices; this model supplies the closures (item 4), not its cost.

## Avoided emissions, valued, and warming

Against 2029 current law, the decided set avoids about 28,164 Mt CO2e over 2030-2050, 25.31 Gt of it CO2. **Valuation (a labeled side table, not booked):** at EPA's 2023 social cost of carbon (2% near-term discount rate, $230 a ton in 2030 rising to $310 in 2050, 2020 dollars; SRC-5006), that is about $7,822 billion of avoided damages, summed without discounting and valuing every gas at the CO2 rate. The second Trump administration's OMB directs agencies not to monetize greenhouse gas effects (M-25-27, SRC-5007) and withdrew the interagency estimates (EO 14154, SRC-4732); this table is Project 2050's labeled valuation on EPA's peer-reviewed 2023 estimates, not federal guidance. **Warming:** at IPCC's 0.45°C per 1,000 Gt CO2 (likely 0.27-0.63; SRC-5037), the avoided CO2 is about 0.0114°C (0.0068-0.0159); methane's shorter-lived warming is not converted.

**Weather in the starting year.** NOAA's degree days (SRC-5047, SRC-5048) put 2025 at 97% of the 2015-2024 heating average and 106% of the cooling average, so the engine's 2025 calibration needs no weather adjustment beyond a few percent of buildings CO2 (EIA's "colder winter" was colder than 2024's, not than normal).

45Q in 2025 $ billion, calendar years. Retrofits' 45Q is in the engine's credits; 45Q on new capture plants and industrial capture is reported only (the ledger books current-law 45Q outside this model). "Stacking" (`q45Stack`) pays 45Q on top of the carbon price a stored ton avoids; the other runs pay the larger of the two, the engine's default. A coal unit with a retrofit under way is not retired if the retrofit will meet the power plant standard (capture of at least 90%, CLI-4R.01); at 75% capture in operation it cannot, so under the standard no coal retrofit starts.

**EP-1 and EP-2, the curves** (net greenhouse gases, Mt CO2e, land use included as each model books it). Espen's EPS runs of the plan's settings (EPS 4.0.7, 2026-11-13) beside this engine's runs of the same settings; each model's cut is against its own current-policy run, since the two models start from different totals:

| Year | EPS current policies | EPS run 1, price | EPS run 2, package | Engine current policies | Engine, price | Engine, package | Cut, price: EPS / engine | Cut, package: EPS / engine |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2030 | 5,144 | 4,858 | 4,606 | 4,986 | 4,447 | 4,434 | 285 / 539 | 538 / 552 |
| 2035 | 4,958 | 3,996 | 3,618 | 4,712 | 3,920 | 3,779 | 962 / 792 | 1,340 / 933 |
| 2040 | 4,637 | 3,682 | 3,178 | 4,480 | 3,466 | 3,153 | 955 / 1,015 | 1,458 / 1,328 |
| 2045 | 4,311 | 3,628 | 2,968 | 4,245 | 3,138 | 2,625 | 683 / 1,107 | 1,343 / 1,621 |
| 2050 | 4,364 | 3,431 | 2,778 | 4,051 | 2,903 | 2,191 | 933 / 1,148 | 1,586 / 1,860 |

**Why the differences arise.**

- **DA-1.** The engine is calibrated to these figures, so the pass shows the starting point is right, not that the model predicts. EIA's October Monthly Energy Review revises 2025 to 4,916 Mt (+0.2%).
- **DA-2.** The engine carries EPA's figure; this checks the two have not drifted apart.
- **BL-1.** Gaps 2030 +1.7%, 2035 +1.2%, 2040 -2.1%, 2050 -13.9%. They part after 2040: AEO2026 has power CO2 rising again from 2040 (to 1,042 Mt in 2050, with data-center load and gas build), while the engine keeps retiring coal and adding wind and solar (678 Mt); and the engine's electric-vehicle uptake is faster (1,472 against 1,617 Mt of transport CO2). EIA's own reference cases have missed energy CO2 by 14.6% on average (SRC-5002), so the 2050 gap is inside the range of a baseline's error.
- **EM-1.** One number for how far apart two whole paths are; the year-by-year gaps are in BL-1.
- **BL-2.** Both benchmarks include the 2025 law; Rhodium's lower end assumes high gas prices and slower clean build.
- **BL-3.** Compared as changes from each model's own 2025, because the bases differ: EPS starts at 5,496 Mt with its land sink, the engine at 5,360 Mt (Rhodium's 2025 estimate, 18% below 2005). EPS's baseline includes the 2025 law and later EPA actions (SRC-5017), like this one. After 2040 EPS's emissions level off (4,637 Mt in 2040, 4,364 in 2050) as AEO2026's do (BL-1), while the engine keeps falling.
- **PK-1.** The EPS package is far wider and has no carbon price: the IRA's credits restored through 2050, a clean standard of 76% in 2035 and 95% from 2040, federal and state vehicle sales standards from 2031, building electrification and efficiency standards, about 150 industrial electrification and 100 efficiency settings, a 50% low-carbon fuel standard, methane capture, land, farm and forest measures, and direct air capture and rock weathering of roughly 370 Mt a year by 2050 (SRC-5044; the run's settings file). The decided set leaves farms and forests as booked, adds no carbon removal, and its industry and building measures are fewer. The gap shows what those extra measures would have to do; it is not a test of either model.
- **EP-1.** This model's cut is 189% of EPS's in 2030, 82% in 2035 and 123% in 2050: about the same size over the period, with a different shape. This engine cuts more at first, because its power plants switch from coal to gas as soon as the price makes coal dearer. The regional fuel price spread (HI-1) slows that switching but does not remove the gap: from 2020 to 2021, when gas prices doubled, measured coal power rose 16% while the engine's roughly doubled. Part of that was the coal shortage, which annual data cannot separate out, so the engine's first-year power response is likely still too strong; monthly or plant-level history would settle it. EPS's cut comes mostly in 2031-2035, as plants retire, new capacity is built and carbon capture is fitted to existing coal and gas plants (EP-3), and then levels off, while this engine's keeps growing as the price rises 5% a year and equipment turns over. Methane and fluorinated gases are priced in both runs, as EPS's defaults do.
- **EP-2.** This model's cut is 102% of EPS's in 2030, 70% in 2035 and 117% in 2050: about the same size over the period, with a different shape. The settings differ where the sliders allowed: EPS's construction subsidies start in 2026, its sales standards also cover buses, motorbikes and light trucks, its building electrification covers appliances too, and its methane capture covers coal mines and landfills; this model's standards also retire unabated coal by 2040. EPS's package cut is larger through 2040 and this model's larger by 2050, the same pattern as EP-1.
- **EP-3.** Both models start 2030 with about the same coal under current policies (524 and 546 TWh), so the difference is the response, not the starting fleet. In 2030, the price's first year, this engine runs 88% less coal and has already added 308 TWh of wind and solar, because its investors build ahead on the expected price; EPS runs 51% less coal and adds none yet. Its coal-to-gas switching in the first year is likely too strong (HI-1). By 2035 both have added about the same wind and solar (724 and 716 TWh). The difference is carbon capture: EPS fits it to existing coal and gas plants, 762 TWh in 2035 (396 from coal), so its gas and coal burn without capture falls far faster. This engine now has a retrofit option (assumptions.csv, ccs_retrofit_*), but on EPA's costs (IPM Table 6-2: a third of a coal unit's output lost, 44% more fuel per MWh), 75% capture in operation (Boundary Dam 3 managed at most 63% a year) and about seven years to build, no retrofit pays under this price before the late 2030s, so the engine builds none here (67 TWh of capture, all on new gas plants). Run on EPS's own retrofit terms as read from its code, unverified (95% capture, no capacity lost, one year to build, every plant eligible), the same engine's price-only run cuts 1,048 Mt by 2035 instead of 792 (768 TWh from retrofitted plants), against EPS's 962: those terms alone more than close the 2035 gap between the two models (151% of it). Retrofitting most of the coal fleet within five years is far beyond anything built so far, so EPS's 2035 power cut leans high on that count.
- **PR-1.** The engine sits in the range's lower half, as its own validation found against NEMS, REGEN and E3 (SRC-0077, v2.3): it responds slowly in the first decade, so its receipts lean high and its cuts lean low. EMF 37's prices are in 2018-2020 dollars, the engine's in 2025 dollars.
- **PR-2.** +26%, about the same in every year (FY2025 $71B against CBO's $53B; FY2034 $148B against $118B). The gap is in the level from the first year, not in the speed of the cuts: CBO's FY2026 receipts are 83% of the engine's, and on gasoline alone, the fuel least able to respond in a year, 85% (CBO's alternative without gasoline gives $18.0B less in FY2026; the engine's light-duty vehicle CO2 stands in for gasoline's). The ratio then falls slowly to 80% by FY2034: the engine's base does shrink a little more slowly than CBO's, but that adds only a few points over the decade. Most of the gap is there from the first year: CBO counts about a sixth less revenue per ton taxed, on every fuel. Its notes don't say why; candidates are a larger offset or compliance and collection allowances in JCT's conventions, or a narrower base (feedstocks, exports). The legacy ledger set REV-C1's midpoint about 5% below the model (ledger-revenue.csv, C1). An earlier version of this note put the whole gap down to slow first-decade cuts; the year-by-year ratio shows that is the smaller part. CBO covers energy CO2 and some large manufacturers' other gases from 2025; the engine prices fuel CO2 and industrial process CO2 and N2O, and starts its price with no warning (CBO's estimate is static apart from the offset).
- **CR-1.** Not like for like: the IRA's credits ran from 2023 with twelve years to 2035 and longer terms; these start in 2030; the household credits step down from 2035 and the power credits to 60% for projects starting 2035-37 (CLI-1A.02); and grid access, not cost, limits wind and solar building (SRC-0077, v2.4).
- **BI-1.** Their figures are total household energy spending, including fuel; this is the electricity price alone.
- **BK-1.** Shows the engine's new options default to the old behavior and the accounts read the engine as carbon-model.py does; the drift check on the legacy outputs shows the same from the other side.
- **BK-2.** Memo 1 scaled the legacy model's receipts by power and industry's share; this runs the narrower price, so buildings and non-road fuel respond as unpriced sectors and industry pays on its covered share.
- **DI-1.** A shape test: the levels depend on the coverage and on the 20% that does not return as the dividend.
- **HI-1.** Total fossil generation is right by construction; the test is the split between coal and gas. With one national fuel price the engine switched the whole fleet at once (average gap 9.1%). The dispatch now splits each block of plants by the spread of fuel prices EIA measures across states (30% of the average price for coal, 20% for gas; SRC-5058 to SRC-5061) times a labeled calibration of 1.5 (assumptions.csv, fuel_spread_mult). That roughly halves the gap but does not close it. An earlier version left out 2021-22 for the coal shortage EIA documents (SRC-5062, SRC-5063). The monthly run (HI-2) does not support that: the same over-response appears, in the other direction, in months when stockpiles were full, and the stockpile adds nothing once prices are counted. So every year is scored, and the check fails. The engine still switches between coal and gas too readily when prices move; a carbon price works through the same switch, so its near-term power cut leans high (EP-1, EP-3). The full-engine history run (vehicles, buildings and building decisions from 2015) is still to be built. **Damped switching, tested and not adopted** (`coalDamp` 0.6, assumptions.csv `coal_damp`): letting plants move only 60% of the way from last period's dispatch toward this period's narrows the yearly gap to 5.2% (still a fail) and the monthly gap to 6.9%, but only on the cheap-gas side (-8.2% in those months; +7.4% when gas is dear, nearly unchanged). It also cuts the engine's short-run elasticity of coal-and-gas CO2 to the gas price from 0.26 to 0.16; the published estimates the M4 research noted (Knittel, Metaxoglou and Trindade, NBER w21627, 2015) are to be checked before any damping is adopted. The remaining gap sits mostly in 2021-22, the dear-gas, short-coal months, where a lag cannot help.
- **HI-2.** The gap moves with the gas-to-coal price ratio: its logarithm alone explains 89% of the month-to-month gap (+19.5 points per unit). Adding the coal stockpile's shortfall from its usual level for the month leaves the fit at 90% (+0.07 points per million tons): once prices are counted, the 2021-22 shortage explains little, though the two moved together (stocks were lowest when gas was dearest), so annual data could not tell them apart. So the engine's coal-gas switching is too strong in both directions, not only when coal was short. A test of one cause, coal bought under take-or-pay contracts (fuel cost sunk in the short run), improved the monthly fit from about 8% to 6% at a 30% contracted share, but the 2025 recalibration then put coal's running cost at $9-14/MWh, above published figures; it is not adopted until the contract evidence is in. February 2021 (Winter Storm Uri, gas at $17) is shown but left out of the fit.
